titulo.texto: The Origin of the Cult and the Nican mopohua

frase_gancho.texto: The memory of faith and the documents, told separately.

puente_narrativo.texto: You are still in the same place, now to see how the origins of the sanctuary are told.

guion_corto.texto: Guadalupan tradition holds that in December of fifteen thirty-one the Virgin Mary appeared to Saint Juan Diego on this hill. That is the memory of faith, and it is the origin of the sanctuary. The surviving documents show another part of the story. A text from fifteen fifty-four already mentions a hermitage at Tepeyac. In sixteen forty-eight the first extensive account was printed in Spanish, and in sixteen forty-nine the Nican mopohua, in Nahuatl. Historians debate when the latter was written. Both things, the memory and the documents, make up this story. The sanctuary is born from the first and is documented in the second.

guion_largo.texto:
The story of the sanctuary can be told in two ways, and both are part of what you see here.

The first is that of Guadalupan tradition. According to it, in December of fifteen thirty-one the Virgin Mary appeared several times to an Indigenous man named Juan Diego, on this hill. She asked him to go to the bishop, Friar Juan de Zumárraga, and tell him that she wanted a temple in this place. As a sign, the image of the Virgin was left on Juan Diego’s tilma. That is the memory of faith, and because of it this sanctuary exists. The Church recognizes the cult. Saint Juan Diego was beatified on the sixth of May, nineteen ninety, and canonized on the thirty-first of July, two thousand two, in this Basilica.

The second is the one told by the documents. The earliest surviving one that mentions the hermitage at Tepeyac dates from fifteen fifty-four, by the humanist Francisco Cervantes de Salazar. In fifteen fifty-six, Archbishop Alonso de Montúfar opened an inquiry into the cult. It included two sermons, that of Montúfar and that of the Franciscan provincial Francisco de Bustamante, who held different views on the devotion. Both expressed different opinions about the devotion.

The texts that recount the apparitions in detail date from the seventeenth century. In sixteen forty-eight, the priest Miguel Sánchez published a book in Spanish about the image. In sixteen forty-nine, Luis Lasso de la Vega, vicar of this sanctuary, printed a work in Nahuatl that includes the Nican mopohua, the account of the apparitions that is known to this day. The first words of the text give it its name.

For decades, historians have debated when and by whom the Nican mopohua was written. Some place it in the sixteenth century, at times with Antonio Valeriano as its author. Others place it in the early seventeenth. That debate remains open. Nor does any document survive from the first half of the sixteenth century that speaks of Juan Diego, although oral tradition has kept him alive. All of this is what is known today.

The cult grew over time. In seventeen thirty-seven Mexico City swore an oath to the Virgin of Guadalupe as its patroness, in seventeen forty-six she became patroness of all New Spain, and Pope Benedict the Fourteenth confirmed it in seventeen fifty-four.

Those who live their faith from this tradition see in it an event. Those who study the documents see a historical process. Both views coexist in this place, and both explain why Tepeyac became a pilgrimage center for millions of people.

If you look toward the hill, you will see the chapels that were built over the centuries. The next stops will take you to see them.
